source_refs.note: Topic 21.3.1 (PDF 79-81); the SN2, SN1 and carbocation diagrams are redrawn. The book says primary and tertiary halogenoalkanes 'always' follow SN2 and SN1; the lesson says they react by these mechanisms.

blocks.text: Nucleophilic substitution involves two processes: the leaving group departs (the C-X bond breaks) and the nucleophile attacks (the C-Nu bond forms). If both happen together in one step, the mechanism is SN2. If they happen in two separate steps, bond breaking first and bond making second, the mechanism is SN1.

SN2 is a single-step mechanism. As soon as the nucleophile begins to attack the electrophilic carbon, the bond to the leaving group begins to break; bond formation and bond breaking go together. The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group.

blocks.alt: OH- with a curly arrow to the delta+ carbon of bromomethane (H3C-Br, delta- on Br), attacking from the side opposite Br, and a curly arrow from the C-Br bond to Br. Then the bracketed transition state HO---C---Br with a negative charge, then methanol with its three H atoms flipped to the other side (delta- on O, delta+ on C) + Br-.
blocks.caption: SN2 mechanism: bromomethane and hydroxide ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 79).

blocks.text: Because two molecules take part in this one (rate-determining) step, the reaction is bimolecular, and its rate depends on both concentrations: rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile], so it is second order (1 + 1 = 2).

Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2 when attacked by nucleophiles. This is for steric reasons: the carbon carries hydrogen atoms or only one alkyl group, so the nucleophile can reach and attack it easily.

SN1 has two steps. First the halogenoalkane ionises reversibly, in a solvent such as aqueous acetone or aqueous ethanol, giving a carbocation intermediate. Second, the nucleophile attacks the carbocation to give the product. The first step breaks a covalent bond, so it is slow; the second, the combination of oppositely charged ions, is fast. The slow first step is rate-determining and involves only one molecule, so the mechanism is unimolecular: rate = k[halogenoalkane], first order.

blocks.alt: First Step: (H3C)3C-Br, delta+ on C and delta- on Br, with equilibrium arrows marked slow, gives the planar carbocation (labelled Carbocation) + Br-. Second Step: the carbocation + OH-, with a curly arrow from OH- to the positive carbon, fast, gives (H3C)3C-OH, labelled Product.
blocks.caption: SN1 mechanism (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 80).

blocks.text: Tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1 when attacked by nucleophiles. The main reason is that they form a stable tertiary carbocation; also, three bulky groups on the electrophilic carbon prevent the nucleophile from attacking from the back of the leaving group. A secondary halogenoalkane can react by either SN2 or SN1, depending on the solvent.

blocks.alt: Four carbocations in order tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl. Each positive carbon is drawn with its groups; red arrowheads on the bonds from CH3 groups point to the carbon. The tertiary has three CH3 groups, the secondary two, the primary one and the methyl carbocation none.
blocks.caption: Decreasing stability order of carbocations due to decrease in positive inductive effect (+I) (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 80).
